opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think it comes down to how I see the work itself. A paper is the product of a whole team: the people who ran the experiments late at night, who debugged the infrastructure, who cleaned the data, who argued through the design choices. When I'm leading a team, my role is more about setting direction, removing obstacles, and making sure people have the resources and space to do their best work. If my name sits on every paper, it can quietly shift the credit toward me, and I don't think that reflects where the real effort went.

There's also a practical side. Young researchers build their careers on visible contributions. If their names stand out more clearly, without a senior name that people automatically associate with the result, that helps them get recognized, invited to give talks, and trusted with bigger problems. I'd rather the outside world learn who these people are.

And personally, I'm just not very attached to that kind of visibility. What motivates me is whether the model works, whether we pushed something forward. Seeing the team grow and seeing the results speak for themselves is more satisfying to me than seeing my name in an author list. So leaving it off feels natural, not like a sacrifice.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I don't think of it as some deliberate principle. It's more about how I see my own role on the team.

When I'm leading a project, most of the real work is being done by the people actually running experiments, debugging the training pipeline at two in the morning, reading the loss curves line by line. My job is more about setting direction, deciding what's worth trying, and clearing obstacles so they can focus. That's valuable work, but it's a different kind of contribution from writing the paper itself. If I put my name at the front, it can dilute the credit that should go to the people who did the heavy lifting, especially younger researchers who need that recognition far more than I do at this point.

There's also a cultural thing I care about. In a lot of labs, the hierarchy gets baked into the author list, and over time people start optimizing for where their name lands instead of for whether the model is actually better. I'd rather the team feel that the result belongs to everyone, and that the paper is a record of the work, not a ranking of people. When I step back from the byline, it sends a small but clear signal about what matters.

And frankly, I've already had my share of first-author papers earlier in my career. I know what that feels like, and I don't need it again to feel like I did something. If a model we built gets used widely and the people on the team grow into stronger researchers because of it, that's the credit I actually want.
